create.title: Create a pool
create.name: Pool name
create.nameHint: Lowercase letters, digits, - and _; starts with a letter.
create.noDisks: No disk can be used right now.
create.refused: {count, plural, one {# disk is} other {# disks are}} not available
create.commands: These commands would run, exactly as shown:
create.notYet: Creating pools from here comes with the next update. Nothing was run.
create.blocked: Not every chosen disk can be used:

recommend.single: With one disk there is no protection: when it fails, the data is gone. Keep a backup.
recommend.mirror: For {count} disks we recommend a mirror: every disk holds everything, so all but one may fail.
recommend.raidz1: For {count} disks we recommend RAID-Z1: one disk may fail, and all others hold data. It works like RAID 5.
recommend.raidz2: For {count} disks we recommend RAID-Z2: two disks may fail, which matters because rebuilding large disks takes long. It works like RAID 6.

wizard.mixedSizes: The disks differ in size: every disk counts as large as the smallest, so {wasted} stay unused.
wizard.drawing: {data, plural, one {# disk} other {# disks}} for data, {protection, plural, =0 {none for protection} one {# for protection} other {# for protection}}

tolerance.none: No disk may fail: one failure loses everything.
tolerance.any: {count, plural, one {Any # disk may fail.} other {Any # disks may fail.}}
tolerance.pairs: One disk per pair may fail, up to {max} in total.

wizard.summary: {layout} of {count, plural, one {# disk} other {# disks}}, about {usable} usable, not encrypted.

encryption.question: Should the pool be encrypted?
encryption.explain: Encryption can only be chosen now, when the pool is created. It cannot be switched on later: the pool would have to be created again and its data copied back.
encryption.noneHint: Anyone with the disks can read the data. Fine for media and backups of other encrypted data.
encryption.keyLater: Comes with the key vault in the next update. To encrypt this pool, wait for it: a pool created now stays unencrypted.

single.title: Single disk
single.goodFor: Good for: trying things out, data that also lives elsewhere.
single.fixed: Can be turned into a mirror later by attaching a second disk.

mirror.title: Mirror
mirror.goodFor: Good for: two disks, the most important data, fast reading.
mirror.fixed: More disks can be attached to the mirror later; the space stays that of one disk.

mirrors.title: Mirror pairs
mirrors.goodFor: Good for: speed, virtual machines and databases; grows two disks at a time.
mirrors.fixed: Grows by adding another pair. A pair whose two disks fail loses everything.

raidz1.title: RAID-Z1
raidz1.goodFor: Good for: most homes, the most space with one disk of protection.
raidz1.fixed: The protection level stays at one disk. Disks can be added one at a time later (RAID-Z expansion).

raidz2.title: RAID-Z2
raidz2.goodFor: Good for: six disks or more, large disks, data that must survive two failures.
raidz2.fixed: The protection level stays at two disks. Disks can be added one at a time later.

raidz3.title: RAID-Z3
raidz3.goodFor: Good for: many large disks and archives where three failures must be survived.
raidz3.fixed: The protection level stays at three disks. Disks can be added one at a time later.

stripe.title: Stripe
stripe.goodFor: Only for: scratch space whose loss does not matter.
stripe.fixed: Protection can never be added. One failed disk loses the whole pool.

actions.datasets: Everything on the pool is lost, including these datasets:

replace.title: Replace {device}
replace.explain: The new disk takes the place of {device} in {pool}; ZFS copies the data onto it (resilver). A new disk is never used on its own.
replace.serialHint: Type the serial number printed on the disk to confirm it is the one you mean.

spareAdd.title: Add a hot spare to {pool}
spareAdd.explain: A hot spare waits in {pool}; when a disk fails, ZFS rebuilds onto it right away.

spareRemove.title: Remove the spare {device}
spareRemove.explain: {device} stops being a hot spare of {pool}.

offline.title: Take {device} offline
offline.explain: {pool} stops using {device}, for example to swap it. The pool stays usable if it has protection left.

online.title: Bring {device} online
online.explain: {pool} uses {device} again and rebuilds what it missed.

destroy.title: Destroy {pool}
destroy.explain: The pool {pool} and all its data are deleted. This cannot be undone.

datasets.title: {count, plural, one {# dataset} other {# datasets}}
datasets.intro: Every pool keeps its data in datasets (file systems) and volumes (block devices for virtual machines).
datasets.caption: Datasets and volumes of {pool}
datasets.name: Name

volume.label: volume
volume.unprepared: Pithyx did not set up this pool, so it creates no volumes on it.
volume.title: Create a volume on {pool}
volume.explain: A volume is a block device, for example the disk of a virtual machine. It is created in {parent}.
volume.name: Name
volume.sizeHint: Rounded up to whole 16 KiB blocks, at least 1 MiB.
volume.sparseHint: Reserves no space up front. It can run out of space when the pool fills up, and whatever uses it then sees write errors.

rename.label: Rename {dataset}
rename.title: Rename {dataset}
rename.explain: The dataset keeps its data and stays in {parent}. Its folder moves with the new name, and shared folders in it follow.
rename.listed: These datasets get a new name:

limits.label: Limits for {dataset}
limits.title: Limits and compression of {dataset}
limits.explain: Leave a size empty for no limit. Only what you change is sent.
limits.compressionOnly: This dataset takes only a compression setting: it is a volume, the pool root or part of the Pithyx layout.
limits.quotaHint: The most the dataset may hold, with its child datasets and snapshots. It uses {used} now.
limits.reservationHint: Space kept for this dataset, with its child datasets and snapshots, that nothing else on the pool may use.
limits.compressionHint: Applies to data written from now on. Higher zstd levels save more space and cost more processor time.
limits.recordSizeHint: The largest block of a file. 1 MiB suits large files such as videos, 16 KiB databases; 128 KiB is the default.
limits.invalidNumber: Enter a number, or leave the field empty.

destroy.label: Delete {dataset}
destroy.title: Delete {dataset}
destroy.explain: {dataset} and every file in it are deleted, with its child datasets and all their snapshots. This cannot be undone.
destroy.explainVolume: The volume {dataset} and all its data are deleted, with its snapshots. This cannot be undone.
destroy.listed: These datasets and snapshots are deleted:

snapshots.title: Snapshots
snapshots.intro: A snapshot keeps the state of a dataset at one moment. Users restore files from them under Previous versions in Files. Schedules delete only the snapshots they took.
snapshots.empty: This dataset has no snapshots yet.
snapshots.name: Name
snapshots.schedulesHint: Schedules take one snapshot per hour, day, week (from Monday) or month in UTC and keep the given number of their own snapshots. Held snapshots and snapshots taken by hand or by other tools are never deleted.
snapshots.deleteBody: The snapshot {name} is deleted for good, with every earlier version it holds.
snapshots.typeName: Type the name of the snapshot to confirm
snapshots.rollbackBody: The whole dataset returns to the snapshot {name} of {date}. Every change since then is lost.
snapshots.rollbackNewer: {count, plural, one {This newer snapshot is deleted as well:} other {These # newer snapshots are deleted as well:}}

scrub.title: Scrubs
scrub.intro: A scrub reads every block of a pool and repairs what it can from redundancy.

selfTests.title: SMART self-tests
selfTests.intro: Self-tests run inside the disks. Disks that are asleep are skipped and tried again later, never woken up.

health.intro: Problems Pithyx found, and the scrubs and self-tests that look for them.

sample.standbyHint: Sleeping disks are not woken for status queries.
